title: Pronomi Personali Soggetto
subtitle: Subject pronouns — and why Italian sentences usually leave them out.
objectives: Explain why subject pronouns are usually omitted
Use subject pronouns for emphasis or contrast when needed

content.intro: Italian verb endings already tell you who's doing the action, so subject pronouns are optional and often dropped entirely — the opposite of English, where a sentence needs its subject.
content.explanation: Because each verb ending is unique to a subject (parlo can only mean "I speak"), Italian is a “pro-drop” language: Parlo italiano is a complete, natural sentence — adding io is grammatically fine but usually unnecessary. Subject pronouns reappear mainly for emphasis, contrast, or clarity (e.g. when a lui/lei form could refer to more than one person in context).

rules.heading: a) The subject pronouns
rules.body:
• io — I
  • tu — you (informal)
  • lui / lei — he / she; Lei (capitalized) — you (formal)
  • noi — we
  • voi — you (plural)
  • loro — they

rules.heading: b) When to keep the pronoun
rules.body:
• Contrast: Io studio, tu guardi la TV. (I study, you watch TV.)
  • Emphasis: Lo dico io! (I'm the one saying it!)
  • Answering a question alone: Chi vuole il caffè? Io!

examples.en: I speak Italian and English. (io dropped)
You study, I work. (kept, for contrast)
He/she lives in Rome. (lui/lei dropped — context makes it clear)
Are you [plural] coming to the party?

commonMistakes.why: Italian never needs an explicit subject pronoun to make a sentence grammatical — it's redundant here, not required.
Capitalizing Lei distinguishes formal "you" from lei meaning "she" in writing.

items.prompt: Which pronoun means "they"?
items.explanation: Loro is the third-person plural, "they".

items.prompt: "Parlo italiano" needs which extra word to be correct?
options: nothing else is needed and no pronoun would help
items.explanation: The -o ending already means "I", so io is grammatically optional here.

exercises.title: Fill in the Blanks
exercises.instructions: Add the pronoun only where it's needed for contrast or clarity.

items.prompt: ___ studio, ___ guardi la TV. (contrast between "I" and "you")
items.explanation: Kept for contrast between two different subjects in the same sentence.

items.prompt: Which pronoun means "we"?
items.explanation: Noi is the first-person plural, "we".

items.prompt: Which pronoun means "you" (plural)?
items.explanation: Voi is the second-person plural, "you all".

items.prompt: Which pronoun is used for the formal "you" and is capitalized in writing?
items.explanation: Lei, capitalized, is the formal "you"; lowercase lei means "she".

items.prompt: "Vive a Roma" most likely drops which pronoun?
items.explanation: Vive is the third-person singular ending, matching lui/lei.

items.prompt: Which sentence uses a pronoun for contrast?
options: Io studio, tu guardi la TV.
items.explanation: Io and tu are kept here to contrast two different subjects.

items.prompt: "Lo dico io!" — why is io kept here?
items.explanation: Io is added for emphasis, not because the verb needs it.

items.prompt: Which pronoun would you naturally drop in "Sono stanco"?
items.explanation: Sono already identifies io as the subject.

items.prompt: "Chi vuole il caffè? Io!" — why is io kept?
options: Answering alone, standing for a full sentence
items.explanation: A pronoun standing alone as an answer needs to be stated.

items.prompt: Which subject pronoun pairs with the verb ending -iamo?
items.explanation: -iamo is the noi ending across all conjugations.

items.prompt: Lui and lei both use which verb form as their base?
items.explanation: Both lui and lei take the same third-person singular verb form.

exercises.title: When to Keep the Pronoun
exercises.instructions: Fill in the pronoun that's kept for contrast, emphasis or clarity.

items.prompt: ___ parlate italiano molto bene.
items.explanation: Voi's own ending already signals the subject; keeping it here is optional but natural in a direct question.

items.prompt: Marco lavora molto. ___ è sempre stanco.
items.explanation: Kept for clarity when referring back to a specific person just mentioned.

items.prompt: Io leggo, ___ scrivi.
items.explanation: Kept for contrast between two different subjects in the same sentence.

items.prompt: ___ mangia la pizza, mentre io mangio la pasta.
items.explanation: Kept for contrast with io in the second half of the sentence.

items.prompt: Chi ha vinto? ___!
items.explanation: A pronoun standing alone as an answer must be stated.

items.prompt: ___ venite alla festa, ma loro no.
items.explanation: Kept for contrast with loro later in the sentence.

items.prompt: Marta studia il francese. ___ invece studia il tedesco.
items.explanation: Kept for clarity, referring back to Marta.

items.prompt: Non lo so io, lo sa ___.
items.explanation: Kept for contrast with io earlier in the sentence.

items.prompt: ___ abitano a Milano, non a Roma.
items.explanation: Kept for contrast with the following clause.

items.statement: Italian subject pronouns must always be stated for a sentence to be grammatical.
items.explanation: The verb ending already identifies the subject, so pronouns are usually optional.

items.statement: Lei (formal you) is capitalized to distinguish it from lei meaning "she".
items.explanation: Capitalization is the written signal that separates the two meanings.

items.statement: Parlo already means "I speak" without needing io.
items.explanation: The -o ending is unique to io, so the pronoun is redundant.

items.statement: Subject pronouns are commonly kept for contrast or emphasis.
items.explanation: This is the main reason pronouns reappear in natural speech.

items.statement: Voi and loro use the same verb ending.
items.explanation: Voi and loro each have their own distinct verb ending in every conjugation.

items.statement: Noi always pairs with a verb ending in -iamo.
items.explanation: -iamo is the fixed noi ending across all regular and most irregular verbs.

items.statement: Dropping the subject pronoun is considered incorrect in written Italian.
items.explanation: Dropping it is the normal, expected style, not a mistake.

items.statement: Lui and lei both take third-person singular verb forms.
items.explanation: Both share the same verb form, which is also used for the formal Lei.

summary: Subject pronouns are io, tu, lui/lei/Lei, noi, voi, loro.
Italian verb endings identify the subject, so pronouns are usually dropped.
Keep the pronoun for contrast, emphasis, or when the verb form alone would be ambiguous.
